title: Behar: the land rests (Leviticus 25:1–7)
hook: every seventh year the land lies fallow and its produce is open to all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emor ended with one law for the stranger and the home-born. Your line was one law for all. Did you use the same rule for a newcomer? Today, a new portion, and a Sabbath for the soil. Day four hundred twenty.

Here is the instruction to a farmer: for one whole year out of every seven, don't sow. Don't prune the vines. Don't harvest the way you normally would. Whatever grows by itself becomes food for everyone, including the hired workers, the settler, and even the wild animals. On paper, it sounds like a recipe for hunger. In modern Israel, farmers and rabbis still wrestle over how to keep it. And the Torah opens the portion with a strange address: it says this was spoken at Mount Sinai.
screen: `ONE YEAR IN SEVEN: DON'T PLANT.` → `ANYONE MAY TAKE.` → `SPOKEN AT MOUNT SINAI.`

segments.voice: First, the law. When you come into the land, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD." Six years you sow and harvest. The seventh is the year tradition calls shmita, a release. The land lies fallow. Second, who eats. What grows on its own is for everyone: you, your servants, your hired worker, the settler living with you, your cattle, and the wild animals in your land. For a year, the owner's fence means less. The rich farmer and the poor stranger eat from the same field. Third, why Sinai? Rashi asks: what does the sabbatical year have to do with Mount Sinai? Weren't all the commandments given at Sinai? His answer: just as shmita was given with its general rules and its fine details at Sinai, so were all the others. Fourth, the week behind us. As yourself closed Kedoshim. Emor said it twice, set the appointed times, counted fifty days, fed the poor at the feast, and gave one law for all. Now Behar, on the mountain, lets the ground rest. Shmita is still observed in Israel, in different ways in different communities. In other places, people borrow its rhythm: a sabbatical, a fallow season, a year of letting something lie.
screen: `SHMITA: THE SEVENTH-YEAR RELEASE.` · `THE FIELD IS OPEN TO ALL.` · `WHY SINAI? RASHI ASKS.` · `A WEEK FROM KEDOSHIM TO BEHAR.` · then, large: `THE LAND RESTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing lie fallow. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that's been worked every single day, without a break. Your body. A relationship you keep managing. A project. A habit of always optimizing. What would it mean to let it rest, for a day, a week, a season? Not to abandon it. To leave the soil alone so it can recover. Choose one thing you'll let lie fallow for a while. The bell holds the time.
Shmita. The release: the seventh year, when the land of Israel rests and what grows is open to everyone, people and animals alike.
Your line: the land rests too. Today, leave one thing unworked, and see what grows without you. Day four hundred twenty, and another week behind you.

howItsDone: In Israel the shmita year is observed by some farmers and consumers, through fallowing, special arrangements for produce, or a contested legal sale of land; outside Israel, Jews study its laws and some communities mark the year with learning and giving.

trapdoor: what you thought: farmers taking a year off.
what it means: a Sabbath for the land, when ownership loosens and everyone eats from the field.

what a scholar hears: Leviticus 25:1–7 sets the land's sabbath; the noun shmita (release) comes from Deuteronomy 15, and Exodus 23:11 uses its verb; Rashi's 'what has shmita to do with Sinai?' comes from the Sifra.

sources.quoted: then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 25:2 'then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD.' quoted from memory; confirm.
The noun 'shmita' appears in Deut 15:1–2 (release of debts); Exodus 23:11 uses the verb (tishmetenah). Lev 25 itself speaks of the land's sabbath. Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Modern observance: heter mechira (sale permit), otzar beit din, and other arrangements are debated; howItsDone says 'contested legal sale'. Confirm tone.

Editor review (y2 judaism 407–425): hook no longer opens 'Imagine' and names the settler (toshav) as Leviticus 25:6 does, not 'the stranger'; Leviticus 25 never uses the word shmita, so the teach now says tradition calls the year that; cut 'the famous question' and the 'many later teachers: the land belongs to God' line, which also took day 422's angle; week look-back trimmed to this week's days; 'many farmers' softened.
